title: Francis Dana to Robert R. Livingston, St Petersburg, 6 Apr 1783 (O.S.), No. 23: eight lines in Dana's own Lovell-type table (key WIN)

steps.what: Located Dana's No. 23 in NARA PCC item 89 vol. 2 (naId 502963402): MS pp. 727-730, digital objects 312-315; the cipher on p. 730, docketed as the triplicate.
Transcribed the eight lines from the scan (212 tokens); four numbers cut by the frame edge marked n|.

Numbers 1-27 apart from four groups; index of coincidence over periods and alphabet sizes pointed to a 27-sign alphabet and period 3, but the signal is weak (period-3 IC 1.30 x 27 against 1.12-1.23 for other periods); the bigram ranking of the keys (control below) is what finds the key.
Shifts for the three positions found by scoring; in Lovell's convention (key letter = 1) the key word is WIN. Long English runs at each phase.

Aligned the text line by line: three encipherer slips (W positions enciphered with N, N, I), one skipped key position, four cut numbers completed from their first digit, three letters supplied at line ends from the key phase. 201 of 211 letter positions decode directly.

Independent re-reading of the scan and independent decryption script: same 212 tokens, same plaintext; found that the code groups move the key phase irregularly (after 31 and 168, not after 137; 29 opens the text), so the opening [29]n an [31] is not confirmed.

Bigram scores (repository English word list): decryption -2.739; 200 wrong keys with the same alignment best -4.431; all 19,683 period-3 keys on the raw uncorrected stream rank WIN second (WIP first, one letter off) and NWI tenth; 200 shuffles best -4.874.

Wharton V-VI read for the letter and Dana's cipher: No. 23 printed with '(Here follow eight lines of cipher.)'; the 'key ... is missing' footnote belongs to the letter of 1 June 1783 to J. Adams; the scan's P.S. reads 'has come to hand', Wharton 'has not come'. Two web searches found no decipherment.
Code groups 29, 31, 137, 168 considered from context (court, ministry, system); no value adopted, one occurrence each.

Review lead checked after the break: Dana's key sheet in PCC item 59 vol. 1 pp. 137-138 (naId 475671573, images 107-108, Fold3 172700-172701). It is headed 'No. 1': a 25-sign table (a..z without j and v, plus &) in three columns that are not the W, I, N alphabets, and a word list numbered 26-52 (England 29, Holland 31, ... Russia 51, Court 52). It is not the 27-sign WIN scheme of No. 23; 137 and 168 are not on it, and England / Holland do not fit '[29]n an [31] like this'. Verso: 'N.B. When you come to an arbitrary character begin [the] key word again.'

Phase after the code groups re-measured on the raw numbers: after each of 31, 137 and 168 the next letter is under N (liketh..., adopti..., herehe...); W and I give nonsense. So the groups reset the key to N, a fixed restart of the kind the No. 1 sheet's N.B. prescribes. After the opening 29 the text starts under W, which this rule does not explain.

Statistical validation (docs/_validate.py): 204 tokens, 58 types, en-modern order 4: reading -1.921 per letter; random keys -6.754 (z 11.8); key annealed onto shuffled ciphertext best -2.808 (mean -3.025, z 7.4); annealer on the real text -2.786. Verdict: pass.

Brice Dudout's parallel reading (https://bdudout.github.io/europe-chiffree/en/documents.html#dana-1783): he broke the three shifted alphabets blind (frequencies, English 4-grams), then found Dana's table of October 1782 at PCC 89 vol. II p. 656 (alphabets from n, w, i; nomenclator 30-305, three numbers per word; keyword restarts after numbers above 27), whose columns match the break. Values for the open groups: 31 Administration, 137 and 168 Minister, 29 a slip for i. Lines 1-5 agree with the reading here wherever both give a value. The sheet itself not yet viewed here.

Reading review of both entries for No. 23: reading.md and dudout/reading.md read as sentences against their decryptions; four coherent sentences each, completions and code groups marked; grade A recorded on each. Dana's 1782 table sheet was not viewed, so 31, 137 and 168 stay open in the first reading.

Andrew Beling (issue #898, with AI agents) located a transcript copy of Dana's table and of No. 23 in PCC item 109 (naId 2316037): objects 103-104, 'Mr Dana's Cypher' (NARA: 14 Oct 1782), with 'Administration 1 2 3' in block 30-122 (31, 62, 93), 'Minister 7 8 9' in block 123-215 (137, 168, 199), the example 'When the army of America go' and the rule 'begin your Key word anew. # Or to a Cypher above 27'; object 207, a clerk's transcript of No. 23 that gives every number in full: the 208 fully read numbers identical to ours, the four cut numbers 11, 15, 27, 26, the three line ends 20, 11, 1. 29 is in neither the alphabets nor the list. His statement that 216-305 have no words is wrong (next step).

Integration review (AI agent, for the maintainers) opened the NARA images by curl. Dana's own sheet, PCC 89 vol. II p. 656 (naId 502963402, object 262, file 407345), one AI reading at reduced size: alphabets a = 15, 6, 20 and n = 1, 19, 6; Adams 30 61 92, Administration 1 2 3; Franklin 123 154 185, Minister 7 8 9; the example and its numbers; 'This goes by a private & safe hand' (the bearer J. Q. Adams is from Dana's letter at p. 648, not from the sheet). The numbers follow their word (Army 35, America 33; 'America. 33. 64. 95'), so 137 and 168 are Minister. 216-263 are sixteen words, Spanish to Warontzow; 264-305 are blank. Object 207 of item 109 laid beside transcription.txt line by line: 215 numbers, all 208 agree, the seven completed numbers are there. So 31, 137 and 168 are read with the writer's own table and the seven numbers are confirmed from a clerk's copy of the despatch (not the triplicate's own sheet). 29 stays open. reading.md recounted: 52 words, 5 holes (In; is, any, irresistable, influence with a slip or the skipped key position), 0.904: read in part. Not checked: the whole sheet number by number; the other words; which copy the clerk had; the original and duplicate of No. 23. No person has checked an image.

Write-up pass (AI agent, for the maintainers). The clerk's copy of the passage (PCC item 109 p. 202, object 207) transcribed into transcription_item109.txt: eleven lines, 215 numbers. Compared with transcription.txt by script: the 208 fully visible numbers are the same in the same order; the four cut numbers are 11, 15, 27, 26; 20, 11 and 1 stand at the three line ends. So the seven letters the triplicate lacks are in a transcription file.

Page 730 enlarged with no overlay at the doubtful places. The first number is 29: its second figure has the tail of the 9 in the 19 beside it, not the round 3 of the three 23s on the same line. The three numbers Dana wrote in the wrong column (23 in line 1, 12 in line 2, 24 in line 6) are as transcribed, and nothing stands between 7 and 26 in line 5, so the skipped key column is not a lost number. The line ends are as transcription.txt describes them. Recorded in NOTES.md, Transcription doubts.

Dana's sheet (PCC 89 vol. II p. 656, object 262) read at full size and laid beside the clerk's copy (item 109, objects 103-104): the three alphabet columns are headed W, a, r (key word War; WIN is the same key in Lovell's convention); the whole word list transcribed into key.txt, 78 words (Adams 30 to French 60, Franklin 123 to Spain 153, Spanish 216 to Warontzow 231), 264-305 blank. Nothing on the sheet uses 28 or 29, so 29 gets no value from the writer's own key.

Siblings: the leaves next to the cipher in PCC 89 vol. 2 opened (objects 307-319). Pages 723-726 are No. 22 (10 March 1783 O.S.), p. 727 opens '(Tript. No. 23.)', p. 731 opens '(Dupl. No. 24)' of 11 April O.S. No second copy of No. 23 stands here; the original and duplicate were not found.

Print: Wharton V and VI (full text, Internet Archive) searched by script for 'cipher', 'cypher' and for figures inside Dana's letters. Of the 28 letters to Livingston that Wharton prints from No. 9 (14 Oct 1782) to 17 Aug 1783 (counted by script from the OCR text) only No. 23 carries a cipher note; the only other figures are 121 and 134.57 in his letter to John Adams of 1 June 1783. So print gives no second text in this key to try the table on. Wharton prints some letters with omissions, and the manuscripts of the other despatches were not paged through.

Founders Online, read in Chrome (curl and WebFetch get an empty page): the Adams Papers editors read three word numbers in Dana's letters to John Adams with the copy of the cipher Dana sent him, dated 18 Oct 1782 O.S.: 121 Franklin, 134.57 minister of France (1 June 1783), 165.37 minister of Berlin, taken as a slip for 165.57 (6 June 1783). These do not fit the sheet sent to Livingston (Franklin 123, Minister 137 and 168, France 59, Berlin 39): the two copies are numbered differently, and by the editors' values the Adams list seems to begin at 28. Tried on 29: as a word number it starts the key again and the next three numbers give e, o, i. No value for 29. The Adams sheet itself was not seen (Papers of John Adams 13 p. 549, image link dead; Weber 1979 not consulted). The Madison Papers note was opened too (Papers of James Madison 7 pp. 268-272, n. 9): of Dana's three despatches of 6, 11 and 14 April 1783 only eight lines of the first are in cipher, so Nos. 24 and 25 give no second text.

Clear copy looked for: the Adams Papers cite 'MHi: Francis Dana Letterbooks, Official, 1782-1784' for Dana's letters to Livingston; the Massachusetts Historical Society's guide to the Dana Family Papers lists vols. 24-25, Official letterbooks 1781-1784 (microfilm P-646 reel 3), with no digital content (only vol. 23.1, the private letter-book, is online). Dana's own file copy of No. 23 exists and is not online; whether it has the passage in words or in numbers is not known.

Retry and reading review. 29 and the four words with an error of Dana's run again with the full table and the clerk's numbers: same numbers, no new value; all five stay holes. Key replay (replay.py, docs/_replay.py): key.txt applied to the 215 numbers gives 48 of the 52 words of reading.md letter for letter, 4 differ with a mark ([I]n, [i]s, an[y], influ[e]nce), none without; the replay has the two key-column events written in (29 uses one column; one column skipped before the le of irresistable). reading.md read as sentences against decryption.txt and against a second decryption by Dana's rule with nothing corrected: four complete English sentences; 52 words, 5 holes, 0.904; above the short-text floor, so read in part. reading_review grade A recorded; it replaces the review of 14 Nov 2026, made before the file was rewritten.

validation.notes: claimed per-occurrence score -1.921; polyphony 0.0; 8 unread tokens left out; annealer on the real text from random keys reached -2.786

outcome.method_basis: The WIN table was recovered from the eight cipher lines alone (period and alphabet size by index of coincidence, shifts by scoring). The three word codes 31, 137 and 168 are not from the ciphertext: they are read with the writer's own key, Dana's table of October 1782 found in the same volume (PCC 89 vol. II p. 656, Brice Dudout; viewed 24 Nov 2026; clerk's copy in PCC item 109, Andrew Beling), whose three alphabets are the ones recovered. 29 stays without value: it is not in the table.
outcome.fraction_read_source: Tokens: 214 of 215 given a value (211 letter positions, of which 7 cut or missing on the triplicate are taken from the clerk's transcript in PCC item 109, transcription_item109.txt; 31, 137, 168 from Dana's table; 29 open). Words (README rule, recounted 24 Nov 2026 with research/reading_audit/v2_score.py on reading.md, and again by hand in the reading review of the same day): 52 words, 5 holes (In; is, any, irresistable, influence), read_share 0.904. If the seven numbers from the clerk's copy were counted as supplied, 42 of 52 = 0.808. Key replay (replay.json): 48 of 52 words are the key's output, 4 differ with a mark, none without. docs/_check_reading.py on reading.md: readable, clean share 0.8, hole rate 0.07.

gaps.item: group 29 (1 of 215 numbers; the word In)
gaps.detail: not in Dana's table (alphabets 1-27, words from 30); written 29 on the triplicate (seen enlarged) and in the clerk's copy; one occurrence; i is taken from the sentence. Only another copy from Dana's side could settle it: his file copy of No. 23 in the Official letter-books at the Massachusetts Historical Society (Dana Family Papers vols. 24-25; microfilm P-646 reel 3; not digitised), or the original or duplicate of the despatch (not beside the triplicate in PCC 89 vol. 2; not located)

gaps.item: four words with an enciphering error of Dana's: is, any, influence (a letter under the wrong column), irresistable (a key column skipped)
gaps.detail: the numbers are as he wrote them (image, Brice Dudout's transcription and the clerk's copy agree) and the corrections are ours, so the words count as holes; the same letter-book copy, if it has the passage in words, is the only thing that would give them without a correction

texts.label: No. 23, St Petersburg, 6 Apr 1783 (O.S.), PCC 89 vol. 2 p. 730
texts.summary: Dana, waiting in vain for the Russian court to receive him, explains why he cannot predict the outcome: in an Administration not guided by settled principles or system nothing can be counted on, what the Minister adopt in this hour may be opposed by another influence in the next, and properly speaking there is no Minister here. One group (29) is open.
texts.note: Recounted 24 Nov 2026: 52 words, 5 holes (In, from the open group 29; is, any, irresistable, influence, each with a letter Dana enciphered wrongly or after a skipped key position, bracketed in reading.md). Administration and Minister are read from Dana's own table (key.txt). The seven numbers cut or missing on the triplicate are taken from the clerk's transcript in PCC item 109 (transcription_item109.txt, the second transcription file) and are not marked. Dana's spelling kept. Two decryption files: decryption_item109.txt is key.txt applied to the clerk's 215 numbers with nothing corrected (python replay.py; the two key-column events are stated in its header); decryption.txt is the output of decrypt.py on the triplicate, of 27 Oct 2026, which prints the letters after the corrections and lists each correction under the lines.

reading_review.by: integration review of 24 Nov 2026 (AI agent, for the maintainers); not a person
reading_review.note: Grade given by the reviewer, not by the author of the reading; it replaces the grade A of 14 Nov 2026 (Claude, session of 14 Nov 2026), which read the file before it was rewritten on 24 Nov (0.855, four groups open; that review stays in the solution steps and in NOTES.md). reading.md read as sentences against decryption.txt and against a second decryption made for the review, Dana's rule as his sheet states it applied to the 215 numbers with nothing corrected: the two agree, and the reading departs from the key's output only at its five marked places. Four complete English sentences (an Administration not guided by settled principles; what the Minister adopt in this hour may be opposed by an irresistable influence in the next; properly speaking there is no Minister here; hence my present difficulty). Recounted by the README rule: 52 words, 5 holes ([I]n from the group 29, which is not in the table; [i]s, an[y], influ[e]nce, a letter Dana put under the wrong column; irresistab[le], after a key column he skipped), 47 of 52 = 0.904. The text has 52 cipher words, so the short-text floor (under 40 words) does not apply and the 95% bar does: read in part. The reviewer looked at p. 730 enlarged with no overlay (the first number is 29; the three wrong-column numbers are as transcribed; nothing stands between 7 and 26 in line 5) and at the clerk's copy (PCC item 109 p. 202), which gives the seven numbers the triplicate lacks; Administration and Minister were checked on Dana's sheet (p. 656). The key replay (replay.py, replay.tsv) gives 48 of 52 words as the key's output and 4 marked, none unmarked. A model's reading and a model's review: no person has checked it.

texts.label: Dana to Livingston, St Petersburg, 6/17 Apr 1783: independent reading by Brice Dudout with Dana's table of Oct 1782
texts.summary: Brice Dudout's reading of the same eight lines with Dana's own table (PCC 89 vol. II p. 656): the three word codes read as Administration and Minister.
texts.note: His files are kept as he sent them on 27 Oct 2026. State set to read in part on 24 Nov 2026 so that it follows the same README rule as the first entry (a word with a corrected or supplied letter is a hole): by his own marks 9 of the 52 words carry such a letter (‹I›n, ‹i›{s}, an‹y›, {o}r, me{a}sure, {m}ay, in{f}lu‹e›nce, proper{l}y, he{n}ce), 43 of 52 = 0.827, counted by hand; the house counter does not know his marks. The seven letters in { } are since given by the clerk's copy (transcription_item109.txt), which leaves the same places as in the first entry. His own figure is about 98% (209 of his 213 groups would be 0.981; how he counted is not stated in his files).

reading_review.note: Read dudout/reading.md against dudout/decryption.txt. The same four sentences, coherent, with the word codes filled from Dana's table of October 1782 as his README reports (31 Administration, 137 and 168 Minister); deduced letters in braces, corrected slips in ‹›, Dana's spelling kept. The table sheet (PCC 89 vol. II p. 656) was not viewed in this pass, so the three code values rest on the contributor's report.

outcome.notes: Contributed by WAINUT (catalogue 485). The decryption needs ten interventions out of 211 letter positions (three slips, four completed cut numbers, three supplied line-end letters) plus one skipped key position; all are explicit in decrypt.py. No earlier decipherment found; the search was not exhaustive, so first_break = true stands until the MHS Dana Papers and the original and duplicate of No. 23 are checked. The PCC 59 key sheet 'No. 1' was found and checked after the break and is a different scheme, so the method stays ciphertext-only. 24 Nov 2026: Dana's own table (PCC 89 vol. II p. 656) viewed and its copy in PCC item 109 found by Andrew Beling (issue #898): 31, 137, 168 read with it; the seven completed numbers confirmed by the item 109 transcript of No. 23 (a clerk's copy), so that gap is closed; 29 is the one open group. The table reading is Brice Dudout's, the break WAINUT's. All image readings are AI readings. 24 Nov 2026, write-up pass: outcome.key set to recovered (the three alphabets were recovered and are the ones on Dana's sheet; the word list is his own, now in key.txt; 29 is not in the key and cannot be recovered from one occurrence); the five holes each need a copy that is not online (gaps); page docs/dana1783.html written.

prior.where: 24 Nov 2026: the Hawkins transcripts (PCC item 109, naId 2316037) were checked for Dana's table (objects 103-104) and No. 23 (object 207): the transcript gives the cipher numbers, no decipherment. Earlier: Wharton VI (1889) prints the passage as cipher without decipherment; the key sheet 'No. 1' in PCC 59 vol. 1 pp. 137-138 is an earlier, different scheme (checked after the break); the Madison Papers note says it is not decoded there. Wharton VI p. 464 'The key to Mr. Dana's cipher is missing' belongs to Dana to J. Adams, 1 June 1783, not to No. 23. 24 Nov 2026, write-up pass: Wharton V-VI searched in full text (no decipherment; of Dana's despatches from No. 9 on only No. 23 is marked as carrying cipher); the Adams Papers on Founders Online (Papers of John Adams 13 pp. 547-551 and 15 pp. 1-4, 19-21) decode three word numbers in Dana's letters to John Adams with the copy of the cipher sent to Adams and say nothing of No. 23. Not checked: the original and duplicate of No. 23 (not beside the triplicate in the volume, not located), Giunta's The Emerging Nation, Weber 1979 pp. 560-563, and Dana's own file copy of No. 23 in his Official letter-books at the Massachusetts Historical Society (Dana Family Papers vols. 24-25; microfilm P-646 reel 3; not digitised), which may hold the passage in words. A parallel independent reading by Brice Dudout was published the same day as this one (Europe chiffrée, 27 Oct 2026): a blind break of the same three alphabets, then Dana's own table of October 1782 found at PCC 89 vol. II p. 656; neither used the other.
